In this supplement we present the details of our simulation study along with additional results not covered in the main paper.
We first discuss the simulation itself, and then present, in Part I, results for the performance of the point estimates, and finally present, in Part II, results regarding the standard error estimates.

## Simulation Setup

In our simulations, we explore data generating processes (DGPs) that are just beyond the range of scenarios observed in our empirical examples.
Our DGPs follow a classic multilevel modeling structure, with individuals nested in sites.
We first generate sites and site sizes, and then generate the individuals within.
We attempted to roughly mimic the structures we saw in our emperical examples, and consider a variety of scenarios indexed by several factors.
These are:

* the number of sites, $J$
* the expected total number of individuals, $N$,
* the amount of cross site treatment effect variation, $\tau^2$, 
* a three-level factor of whether site size is constant (not varying), whether it varies independently of impact, or whether it varies and is positively correlated with impact.^[For simplicity, we do not consider both positive and negative correlations. We do for proportion treated so we can have the correlations of the two factors be aligned or opposite, causing different aggregate biasing patterns.]
* a four way factor of whether proportion of units treated is constant, or whether it varies and is negatively correlated, positively correlated, or not correlated with average impact of the site.

In presenting our results we reparameterize, and report in terms of the expected average site size of $\bar{N} = N / J$.

We also have some fixed parameters:

* degree of site size variation. For those simulations where site size varies, we allow substiantial variation, with the ratio of the variance of site size to the average site size being set to 0.60, which is the 75th quantile of our emperical datasets.^[We generate random site sizes by sampling from a mixture of uniform distributions, one with probability $p$ ranging from 4 to $\bar{n}-4$ and one from $\bar{n}-4$ to $n_{max}$, with $n_{max}$ and $p$ calibrated to give this ratio.]
* proportion of units treated. The average proportion of units treated in a site is held at 0.65, which many of our emperical examples had.
* variation in proportion of units treated. When the proportion treated varies, they vary from a bit under 50% to a bit over 90% (but all sites are guaranteed to have at least 2 treated and 2 control units).
* ICC. We fixed the ICC (how much of the control-side variation is explained by site) to 0.20, which is at the high end of our estimated ICCs in the emperical data.
* ATE. We fix $\beta_{SP-Sites}$ to be 0.20.

It is possible for the average effect of site, $B_j$, to be both correlated with the $N_j$ (site size) and the $p_j$ (proportion treated), meaning that the sites with the biggest impact tend to be the largest and most lopsided in terms of treatment (in the case of positive correaltion) or largest and least lopsized (in the case of negative correlation).

Under a variety of combinations of these factors we ran a complete factorial experiment, with different levels of $J$, $N$, and $\tau^2$.
These factors along with the two factors governing the relatonship of impact with site size and proportion treated give 448 unique scenarios (we drop the correlated factor combinations with no variation in cross site impacts, as such correlations would be impossible).
For each scenario we simulated in a nested structure so as to be able to estimate finite-sample performance.
That is, we first generated a dataset using a particular DGM.  Each dataset includes, for each observation, the potential outcome under treatment or control.
Then, three times, randomized units to treatment and control, calculated the corresponding observed outcomes, and finally analyzed the results using our full set of methods, recording both the point estimate and estimated standard error for each.^[Three times gives a poor estimate of within-dataset variability, but the average across the 1000 datasets gives a reasonable estimate of expected variability.]
We also recorded, for each generated dataset, the true finite-sample ATE, both person and site weighted.
We repeat this process 1000 times for each given scenario.

For each set of estimates we also record the differences of the point estimates of each method to the four possible estimands (finite or superpopulation ATE weighted by site or person).
(As $\beta_{SP-Persons}$ is not directly calculable, we estimate it for each scenario by taking the average of the finite person-weighted ATEs across all datasets generated by that scenario's DGP.)
These give the actual estimation errors for each estimand.
We will summarize these estimation errors to analyze the performance characterisics of the estimators.


Our simulation study focuses on two general questions: how well the point estimates of the estimators perform *in truth*, and how well the estimated standard errors estimate the true standard errors.
The former question revolves around actual standard error, actual bias, and actual RMSE (root mean squared error) of the estimators with respect to the four estimands.
The latter question revolves around looking at the average and standard deviation of the estimated standard errors for each method, and comparing these estimates to the corresponding true SEs.

## How we calibrated our simulations

The levels of the factors disussed above were roughly selected based on our emperical data.
In particular, we targeted 65% treated to give a lopsided treatment chance, similar to many of our studies, and to allow for bias. Centering treatment at 50% would reduce sensitivity to the bias due to precision-weighting.
We let the proportion vary a bit more than what we saw in the most variable of our emperical examples (the standard deviation of the proportion treated varied from around 0.10 to a max of 0.20, with the largest emperical variation being 0.16).
This allows potentially greater benefits and costs for the fixed effect models that use precision weighting.
(We also include scenarios with no variation in proportion treated to set aside these impacts and concerns.)


We set the ICC to 0.20, which was at the high end of the emperical estimates we had from our studies.
We obtained these estimates using a simple random intercept multilevel model.


We set number of sites and site size to bracket our evaluations, after dropping a very large study with more than 10,000 participants.
We did end up, due to the crossed factorial nature of our study, with some average site sizes much smaller ($\bar{n}_j = 12$, $25$, and $50$) than we saw emperically (with a smallest average of 64).

We calibrated the variation in site size so that the ratio of the site variance to site size squared matched the more variable of our emperical examples.
This is quite a large degree of variation in sites.


The strength of the correlations of site impact to site size and proportion treated, when they are present, are controlled by a single tuning parameter.
We first order true site impacts, site sizes, and proportions treated to share the same rank order, and then shuffle the site impacts to a degree controlled by this single parameter.
We tune this parameter to give emperically observed correlations roughly in line with the higher levels of our actual data (these correlations tended to be small).


Overall, we believe our simulation scenarios to tend towards the more extreme ends of what we saw emperically.
This means the degree of bias and instability is also at the high end; our simulation code is available upon request, however, and exploring other parameter settings would be a good area of future exploration.
We also included scenarios with no variation in site size and/or proportion treated, partially so we could see the impact of one factor when there was no impact from the other, and to ensure that the estimation methods behaved as we expected in these simpler contexts.


# Part I: Investigating actual estimator performance

Although we have many methods, several groups of these methods return the exact same point estimates.
For example, the design based finite sample person weighted estimator gives the same point estimate as the inverse weighted estimator, the interacted linear model estimator, and the design based superpopulation person weighted estimator.
We therefore, in this first overall investigation, limit our attention to the six estimators that give different point estimates; the other estimators give identical point estimates and different estimated standard errors.

The core six estimators we select are design-based person-weighted (DB-Persons), design-based site-weighted (DB-Sites), fixed effects regression (FE), FIRC, RIRC, and RICC.
The first two are unbiased.
The fixed effect estimator attempts to improve precision, but should generally be aligned with the person weighted design based estimator.
The RICC estimator is essentially a version of a FE estimator.
The FIRC and RIRC are adaptive, but targeting site-weighted estimands in principle.
In initial analyses of the estimators we found that RIRC was quite similar to FIRC, and RICC was extremely similar to FE, so we drop them from the presentation of the overall results to reduce clutter in our presentation, and discuss their similarities subsequently.


## Are the methods differently precise?

To examine whether the different methods are differently precise, we examine their true standard errors (we defer issues of estimator bias to subsequent investigations discussed below).
For each given scenario, each estimator actually has two true standard errors: the standard error across all the samples drawn from the superpopulation, and the average finite sample standard error.

The superpopulation true standard error is simply the standard deviation of the point estimates across all simulations within that scenario.
This incorporates the variability due to the sampling process, as it should.

To investigate the true finite-sample standard errors, we take the variance of the three point estimates for the three randomizations within each dataset generated, and then average these over the datasets generated for a given scenario.
This gives the expected true finite-sample variance for a given data generating process (so if the true variance depends on the data itself, such variability would be averaged out, but the variability of the shifting estimands is *not* included in these averaged standard errors).
The square root of this describes how much the estimator tends to vary across randomizations within a set of given, fixed samples with shared heritage (defined by their DGP).

To ease comparisons across simulation scenarios that vary in sample size and, therefore, overall precision, we, for each scenario, standardize the true standard errors by the true (finite or superpopulation, depending on context) SE of the unbiased design-based person-weighted estimator:
\[ inflation = 100\% \times \frac{ SE}{SE_{DB-Persons}} \]
This give the percent differences in the SEs for that context.
We then summarize these percent differences across all the simulation contexts, reporting the middle 90% range of differences to show the range of relative efficienies of a given method to the baseline across simulation scenarios.

Results are on the table, below.
The first pair of columns show average and spread of the percent difference of estimators for finite-sample inference.
The second pair of columns show average and spread of the superpopulation SEs to the superpopulation SE of DB-Persons.
The final pair of columns show the average and spread of the superpopulation SEs to the corresponding finite-sample SE for that same estimator: this shows the increased variability in an estimator due to the variability of the sample.

We see that, for the finite population viewpoint, the site-average design based estimator DB-Sites is more variable than DB-Persons, with a 31% average increase.
The range shows that for some scenarios they can be more than 78% larger, but that in other scenarios there is no difference.
The fixed-effect estimator (and RICC), designed to have higher precision, does in fact have that, but the gains are modest (around 2% on average, with little variation across scenarios.)
Interestingly, FIRC (and RIRC) can also show gains, although they can also be more variable, depending on scenario.
We investigate this pattern of findings a bit futher below.

In the superpopulation context, the site-average design based estimator still has higher SEs.
These relative numbers are muted because the overall variation of everything is inflated by the same amount due to the variability of the samples themselves.
The FE estimator can now actually incur a penalty (although this is small) but FIRC is now actually relatively less variable, on average.

Finally, the final column shows that the true superpopulation standard errors for the various estimators are generally substantially larger than the correpsonding finite sample viewpoint, but there is substantial variability in this.
This variation comes from the different amounts of cross-site impact variation across scenarios: in some circumstances the superpopulation uncertainty is much larger due to this impact variation, and in other circumstances (i.e., when there is no impact variation so the estimands all coincide) the differences are nonexistent.


**Table: Comparing actual SE across methods**
```{r, echo=FALSE}
options(knitr.kable.NA = '')
colnames( SE.table ) = c( "method", "SE (finite)", "90% range", "SE (super)", "90% range", "SE inflation", "90% range" )
knitr::kable( SE.table, digits=0 )
```

**Caption:** Ranges are the middle 90% of the values across all simulation scenarios.


To underscore the roll of cross-site variation in impacts, we plot the relative SEs by this variation, restricting our attention to only those scenarios with variable site size and proportion treated and without correlation biases between site size and proportion treated and site impact.
We see no major trends with one interesting exception: while under the finite perspective, the FIRC method is increasingly relatively variable when there is more cross-site impact variation, but under the superpopulation perspective, the FIRC method is relatively less variable as cross-site impact variation increases.
This is because of the partial pooling: more cross site variation increases the variability, but it increases it slower than the amount of additional variation due to cross site variation, so the relative performance decreases (i.e., improves) when viewed in the superpopulation context.

For the superpopulation side, the apparent reduction in the relative SE of the design based site estimator as cross site variation goes up is a function of all the estimators getting more variable, making the percentage difference less.


**Figure: Percent increase of SE**

```{r percent_increase_SE, echo=FALSE, results="hide"}
mns = mutate( mns, 
             biased = ifelse( method %in% c("FIRC","FE"), "biased", "DB" ) )


mns2 = mns %>% filter( proptx.dependence == "indep", dependence=="indep" ) %>% 
  gather( SE.f, SE.s, key="estimand", value="SE" )
s2 = mns2 %>% ungroup( ) %>% group_by( method, weight, population, tau, weight, proptx.dependence, dependence, estimand ) %>% 
  summarise( mean.SE = mean( SE ) )

table( s2$estimand )

SEnames = c( `SE.f`="SE (finite sample)", `SE.s`="SE (superpopulation)" )
ggplot( s2, aes( x=tau, y=mean.SE, col=method, fill=method, pch = method, lty=method ) ) +
  facet_grid( . ~ estimand, labeller = as_labeller(SEnames)  ) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size=2) +
  labs( y = "Avg Percent Increase of SE", x = expression( tau ) ) +
  scale_shape_manual("", values=c(`DB-Persons`=21,`DB-Sites`=22,FE=23,FIRC=24)) +
  scale_fill_manual("", values = c(`DB-Persons` = "red", FE="red", `DB-Sites`="blue", FIRC = "blue")) +
  scale_color_manual("", values = c(`DB-Persons` = "red", FE="red", `DB-Sites`="blue", FIRC = "blue")) +
  scale_linetype_manual("", values = c(`DB-Persons` = 1, `DB-Sites`=1, FE=2, FIRC=2) ) 

```

**Caption:** The percent increase of the standard error as a function of cross-site impact variation. Only scenarios with no biases between proportion treated or site size and site impact. Left figure are finite-sample, right is superpopulation.

### Comparing FIRC to DB-Super-Sites

In our emperical analysis we identified the most amount variation in estimated standard errors within the domain of the site-weighted, superpopulation estimand.
We wanted to investigate whether these differences are due to different actual standard errors, or instability in estimating standard errors.

We found, in general, that for many scenarios the true SEs of $\hat{\beta}_{FIRC}$ and $\hat{\beta}_{DB-SP-Site}$ were nearly the same, but there were also many circumstances where the design-based estimator was substantially more variable than FIRC.
The average increase was 17%, averaged across all scenarios including those with no variation in site size or proportion treated.
Several scenarios had increases of 50% or more.
We investigate the stability of the estimated standard errors of these two methods below.


```{r droppedblock, echo=FALSE, results="hide", include=FALSE}
if ( FALSE ) {
  
head( mns )
m2 = mns %>% dplyr::select( method, ID, J, n.bar, dependence, proptx.dependence, tau, SE.s ) %>%
  spread( method, SE.s )
head( m2 )
m2 = mutate( m2, ratio = `DB-Sites` / FIRC )
qplot( m2$ratio )
ggplot( m2, aes( tau, ratio ) ) +
  facet_grid( dependence ~ proptx.dependence ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline( yintercept = 1 )

quantile( m2$ratio, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95 ) )
mean( m2$ratio )
}
```



## Are the methods different in terms of their RMSE?

In the prior section we saw some estimators indeed have smaller true SEs than others under some simulation scenarios.
But these estimators are targeting different estimands, which can cloud such comparisons as the SEs are SEs for different quantities.
Furthermore, as we have discussed, some methods exchange bias for increased precision.
We therefore investigate the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of the different estimators to take into account both bias and variance.

To measure the true RMSE we take the square root of the average squared error:
\[ RMSE = \left[ \frac{1}{R} \sum_r \left( \hat{\beta}^{(r)} - \beta^{(r)} \right)^2 \right] .\]
For finite-sample, the $\beta^{(r)}$ will be the finite-sample quantity (person or site average impact), and will vary with the sample.
For the superpopulation context, $\beta^{(r)} = \beta$ across the $R$ simulation trials.
For each method, for each scenario, we will have four values of the RMSE due to the changing $\beta^{(r)}$ for the four different estimands.

We, for each scenario, calculate the four different RMSEs corresponding to our four estimands for each of the estimators, and then compare these RMSEs to the baseline design-based unbiased estimator for that context.
Numbers above 100 mean an estimator is worse (has higher RMSE) by that many percentage points above 100.
Numbers below 100 mean the considered estimator tends to be closer to the estimand.
We, similar to the SE analysis above, average these numbers across all scenarios and also report ranges to show how much variability in the RMSE exists across the scenarios.

We first present the tables and figures of results, and then discuss overall findings.
The table presents the relative increases in RMSE across scenarios.

To examine when the different estimators succeed or fail, we then plot, for each method, the average relative inflation for the different estimators within scenarios grouped by the correlation structure and degree of cross-site impact variation.
We include plots for each of the RMSEs (although these plots are broadly similar in their patterns).


The plots for the person-weighted estimand primarily show how the precision-weighted estimators compare to the unbiased.
The site-weighted plots show how the person-weighted estimators actually outperform the site-weighted in many circumstances due to their reduced variability.
They also show how FIRC compares to the DB-Sites, the unbiased site-weighted design based estimator.

**Table: Relative RMSEs of the estimators as compared to DB-Persons**

```{r RMSE table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable( RMSE.table, digits=0 )
```

**Caption:** Ratio of the RMSE of each estimator to the RMSE for the design based, averaged across all scenarios.  Intervals are middle 90%. The four sets of columns in the table correspond to the four different estimands.


**Caption:** Relative percent increase of RMSE to superpopulation site-weighted design-based estimator. Note that the FIRC method always has lower average RMSE than DB-Sites (there are a small number of high-bias, high-precision scenarios where it is worse). The bias of person-weighting can cause the person-weighted estimators to be worse than DB-Sites, but only in the scenarios with the most extreme cross-site impact variation or scenarios with site impacts correlated proportion treated (for FE).


### RMSE Results


**Person-weighted estimands.**  For the finite population person-weighted estimand (first pair of columns on the table and first collection of plots), we see that DB-Site is reliably the worst choice for the person-weighted estimand (this is unsurprising given its explicit targeting of a different estimand and observed increased variability as illustrated in the SE investigation above; it is both more variable and more biased).
In fact, it can never be superior to the person-weighted, since the weighting by sites can only increase variability and there is no bias to remove.

The fixed effect estimators (FE and RICC), designed to be precision weighted, can outperform the person weighted design-based estimator, but only if there is not substantial bias due to a correlation between  proportion treated and impact.
Furthermore, when there is a great deal of cross-site impact variation, the variable proportion of treated, even if randomly allocated, can cause random amounts of finite sample bias.
Averaged across finite sample scenarios, this can introduce larger average finite-sample RMSE, which is a very surprising result.
From a superpopulation perspective, however, when $p_j$ is independent of $B_j$, we do not see a penalty, just a loss of the potential gains.

The nominally site-weighted FIRC can also outperform the design-based estimator for the person-weighted estimands, likely due to its being a variant of the precision-weighted fixed effect estimator.
For finite-sample RMSE, these gains can easily be lost when there is substantial cross-site impact variation, as the FIRC model will then tend to target the site average impact.


For the person-weighted estimands, the superpopulation stories are roughly the same as finite population.
The relative differences are shrunk due to the additional variation shared by all estimators (the variation of the representativeness of the sample), thus inflating all the RMSEs by a constant amount and making the ratios smaller.
One exception to this is, for FIRC, if there is independence of the $B_j$ and $N_j$ we see increasing gains in superpopulation RMSE with greater cross site variation as the site averaging targets the superpopulation average more effectively (compare these gains to the losses from the finite-sample viewpoint).


**Site-weighted estimands.** Notably, the person weighted DB can outperform the site weighted, even when the target is the site average ATE.
The DB-Sites estimator's great variability when there is substantial variation in site size means that when the site size is not associated with impact, the other estimators that do not seek unbiased estimation can substantially outperform. (See mean.fs and mean.ss columns of the table above.)
In these cases, the person-weighted fully uses the data for no cost.
That being said, if there is such an association, using a person-weighted estimator for a site estimand can increase overall error due to the introduced bias.
Note the ranges for DB-Persons and FE extend beyond 100, showing that there are cases where the precision gains are more than offset by bias.

The FIRC and RIRC models are generally superior to the the unbiased site-targeting design-based estimator, but can also be outperformed if there is substantial cross site variation coupled with a size by impact correlation  (note how the 95 percentile on the table does reach above 100%).
The overall gains are partially due to the adaptive nature of these estimators: when there is no measured cross-site impact variation they tend towards the precision-weighted estimators which are more stable, but when there is cross-site impact variation they adapt to target the site-average effect.
Even when there is substantial cross-site impact variation, the FIRC and RIRC models will always tend towards the person-weighted, thus having enough bias to offset their lower SEs.
This only occurs in the more extreme scenarios.

For site-weighted estimands, the superpopulation stories are again roughly the same as finite population.


## How are the methods differently biased?
We briefly touch on estimator of bias.
We measure average bias as the mean of the errors across all iterations for a scenario.
The average finite-sample and superpopulation bias are both the same.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable( bias.table, digits=2 )
```


```{r, echo=FALSE}

mns2 = gather( mns, bias.fp, bias.fs, key="estimand", value="bias" )
s2 = mns2 %>% ungroup( ) %>% group_by( method, weight, population, tau, weight, proptx.dependence, dependence, estimand ) %>% 
  summarise( mean.bias = mean( bias ) )
s2 = mutate( s2, estimand = fct_recode( estimand, "person" = "bias.fp", "site"="bias.fs" ) )
#mns2 = filter( mns2, dependence =="corr" )
s2 = rename( s2, ptx.dep = proptx.dependence,
             size.dep = dependence )
```


```{r mean_bias, echo=FALSE, results="hide", fig.height=4.5, fig.width = 5 }
s3 = filter( s2,  estimand=="person", size.dep != "const", ptx.dep != "const" )


ggplot( s3, aes( x=tau, y=mean.bias, col=method, fill=method, pch = method, lty=method ) ) +
  facet_grid( ptx.dep ~ size.dep, labeller = labeller( ptx.dep=as_labeller(ptx.names), size.dep=as_labeller(size.names) ) ) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_hline( yintercept = 0 )+ 
  scale_shape_manual("", values=c(`DB-Persons`=21,`DB-Sites`=22,FE=23,FIRC=24)) +
  scale_fill_manual("", values = c(`DB-Persons` = "red", FE="red", `DB-Sites`="blue", FIRC = "blue")) +
  scale_color_manual("", values = c(`DB-Persons` = "red", FE="red", `DB-Sites`="blue", FIRC = "blue")) +
  scale_linetype_manual("", values = c(`DB-Persons` = 1, `DB-Sites`=1, FE=2, FIRC=2) ) +
  labs( y="Mean Bias", x=expression(tau) )


```

**Caption:** Bias for estimators with respect to person-weighted estimand.  Site-weighted biases have corresponding patterns and are therefore not shown. Scenarios with no variation in site size or proportion treated not shown as the biases are similar to independence.


When bias is broken down by scenario type we verify that as cross-site impact variation increases the potential for bias also increases.
The biases for FIRC when the correlation with proportion treated is positive or negative shows that the FIRC model is also precision weighted, just like fixed effects.
We also see some cases where the biases compound, as illustrated by the larger biases in the double-correlated contexts.
The biases can also cancel: see the smaller biases of using the fixed effect estimator for estimating site average impacts when the size correlation is positive and the proportion treated correlation is also positive.


We also examine what percent bias is of the overall RMSE, which also informs how confidence interval converage would go.
We do this by calculating
\[ \mbox{proportion bias} = 100\% \times \frac{ \mbox{bias}^2 }{ RMSE^2 } \]

Across all scenarios we have the following:
```{r, echo=FALSE}
names(bias.table.pct) = c( "Method", "Mean Percent Bias (Person)", "90% range", "Mean Percent Bias (Site)", "90% Range" )
knitr::kable( bias.table.pct, digits=0 )
```

**Caption:** The proportion of overall RMSE that is due to bias, across scenarios. We see that in some scenarios the (squared) bias is a significant fraction of the overall mean squared error. Intervals are the middle 90% of values.


## Discussion

Overall, we have examined scenarios with large amounts of variation in site size and the proportion of units treated.
This variation does mimic that found in many of our emperical examples, however.
This variation provides opportunities for the precision-weighted (e.g., FE) and shrunk (e.g., FIRC) estimators to realize their gains.
On the other hand, if this variation is correlated with impact, as it is in many of the scenarios considered, the bias can offset those gains.

Overall, assuming the estimator and estimand are well selected, we find it is difficult to generate scenarios where gains from fixed effects are larger than 10%, but easy to generate ones where the cost is considerable, even beyond the cost due to a mismatch between a person-weighted estimator being used to target a site-weighted estimand, or vice-versa.

On the other hand, the site-weighted design-based estimator is very suseptible to small sites, making it quite unstable in the face of cross-site impact variation.
The gains of unbiasedness appear to be more than offset by this cost, in general, thus suggesting FIRC is a superior choice in general.



## RICC and RIRC

RICC and RIRC are both nearly identical to FE and FIRC, respectively, and were thus dropped from the above analysis to simplify the presentation of results.
Their relationship to the design based estimators is nearly identical to those of their sisters, FE, and FIRC.
In this section we discuss the differences a bit more explicitly.

### RICC
RICC is basically FE, but with replacing the fixed effect intercept with a random effect intercept.
The point estimates correlate very highly across all simulation runs, with less than 5% of all simulation runs differing by more than 0.01 effect size units.
The largest differences were less than 0.05 effect size units, and 50% of differences were less than 0.002.

We also calculated the relative RMSE across scenarios.
RICC method slightly outperformed the FE estimator, with RMSEs on average of 99.7% of the FE (this slight reduction is, in fact, statisticially significant, indicating a consistent but tiny improvement).
The largest improvements were around a 2% reduction.

### RIRC

RIRC and FIRC differ slightly more than RICC vs FE, but the differences are still far from substantial.
These estimators differ by more than 0.01 around 15% of the time, and more than 0.02 only around 4% of the time.
That being said, for some scenarios these differnences reached upwards of 0.15.
Overall the RMSE performances are quite similar, with RIRC being potentially slightly worse than FIRC, with RMSEs at most 0.4% higher on average.



# Part II: Performance of the estimated standard errors

In Part I we examined the actual performance of the estimates of the Average Treatment Effects.
In Part II we examine how well the uncertainty (the true standard error) is itself estimated.
We now re-introduce the full range of estimators, as even for a given point estimate there can be many ways to calculate a standard error (e.g., cluster robust, heteroskedastic robust, or classic SE estimates for the fixed effect model).

## Are the standard errors calibrated?

We first investigate whether the standard errors of a method equal, on average, the true (appropriately chosen) standard error.
We find that yes, all the methods roughly have standard errors close to the appropriately selected true standard errors.

In the figure below we, for each method, compare the average estimated standard errors to the actual superpopulation standard error and the actual finite population standard error.
These boxplots show the distribution of the ratios across all the simulation scenarios.
We see that the inflation factor hovers around 1 when compared to the appropriate context (finite or superpopulation), with finite population standard error methods systematically underreporting (usually by around 10%, but often 20% or more, in the scenarios considered) the degree of uncertainty for the superpopulation estimand.
The degree of inflation (or deflation) depends on how variable the finite populations are within a given superpopulation context, which is tied to the amount of cross site variation present.
In particular, the right sides of the boxplots on the left (and the left sides of the boxplots on the right) come from those scenarios with maximum cross-site impact variation.

```{r calibratedSEs, echo=FALSE, results="hide"}
inf.names = c( inflate.f = "Inflation (Finite)", inflate.s = "Inflation (Superpop)" )
srun2 = dplyr::select( sruns, method, population, inflate.f, inflate.s, tau, population, J, n.bar ) %>%
  gather( inflate.f, inflate.s, key="estimand", value="inflation" )

ggplot( srun2, aes( x=method, y=inflation ) ) +
  facet_grid( ~ estimand, scales = "free", labeller = as_labeller(inf.names) ) +
    geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() + 
  geom_hline( yintercept = 1, lwd=1,col="red" ) +
  labs( y = "Ratios of average SE.hat to true SE across scenarios", x="")


if ( FALSE ) {

srun2 = dplyr::select( sruns, method, population, inflate.f, inflate.s, tau, population, J, n.bar ) 
srun2 = mutate( srun2, inflation = ifelse( population=="finite", inflate.f, inflate.s ) )
ggplot( srun2, aes( x=method, y=inflation, fill=population ) ) +
  geom_hline( yintercept = 1, lwd=1,col="red" ) + 
  geom_hline( yintercept = c(0.9, 0.95,1.05), col="grey" ) +
    geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() + x
  labs( y = "Ratios of average estimated SE to true SE across scenarios (for appropriate reference SE)", x="")

}
```

**Caption:** On left, comparing the aveage estimated standard error to the true finite-sample standard error, averaged across datasets within each scenario. At right, comparing to the true superpopulation standard error. Note that standard errors are independent of person-weighted vs. site weighted choices.

First, for finite-sample inference, we see some of the standard errors are not as well calibrated as others.
In particular, the standard errors for FE-IPTW-Sites tend to be too small, as do those for FE-Int-Sites and DB-FP-Sites.
We also see that interpreting a superpopulation method's standard error as the standard error for a finite sample estimand is quite conservative.

For superpopulation inference, using a finite sample standard error (e.g., from the fixed effect model) as a superpopulation one is going to be overly optimistic, and lead to poor coverage.
This optimism increases as cross site variation increases.
If there is no cross site variation, there is no bias in the SE estimates as all samples have the same target estimand.
In the $\tau=0.2$ scenarios, the SEs can easily be 40% or more too small.

The superpopulation targeting estimators are quite interesting.
For the ratio of average estimated standard error to true standard error, averaged across scenarios, we have the figure, below, for the superpopulation targeting estimators as a function of cross-site impact variation.
First, we see that the standard errors generally tend to be too small, with the exception of FIRC and RIRC with no cross-site impact variation.
Also note how FIRC and RIRC are giving uncertainty estimates that are increasingly too small in the face of increasing cross site variation.


```{r calibratedSEs3, echo= FALSE, results="hide"}
ggplot( filter( srun2, population == "superpop", estimand=="inflate.s"), aes( x = as.factor(tau), y = inflation ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ method, nrow=1 ) +
  geom_boxplot( fill="grey" ) + geom_hline( yintercept = 1 ) +
      labs( title="Estimated to true SE for superpopulation targeting estimators", x=expression(tau), y="Relative Inflation" )

```

**Caption:** Ratio of estimated SE to true superpopulation population SE for superpopulation targeting estimators for different degress of cross site variation. 1.0 corresponds to correct ratio.


```{r calibratedSEs4, echo= FALSE, results="hide", include=FALSE}
ggplot( filter( srun2, population == "finite", estimand=="inflate.f"), aes( x = as.factor(J), y = inflation ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ method, nrow=1 ) +
  geom_boxplot( fill="grey" ) + geom_hline( yintercept = 1 ) +
      labs( title="Estimated to true SE for superpopulation targeting estimators", x="J (number sites)", y="Relative Inflation" )

```



```{r, include=FALSE}
head( srun2 )
spops.infl = filter( srun2, population == "superpop", estimand=="inflate.s")
table(spops.infl$n.bar)
spops.infl = filter( spops.infl, n.bar >= 50, n.bar < 400 )
table( spops.infl$n.bar, spops.infl$J )
ggplot( filter( spops.infl, tau == 0.2 ), aes( x = as.factor(n.bar), y = inflation ) ) +
  facet_grid( J  ~ method  ) +
  geom_boxplot( fill="grey" ) + geom_hline( yintercept = 1 ) +
      labs( title="Estimated to true SE for superpopulation targeting estimators", x=expression(tau), y="Relative Inflation" )


M0 = lm( inflation ~ method + tau + J + n.bar, data=spops.infl )
summary( M0 )

```


## Are the estimated standard errors differently precise?

For each method, we look at the standard deviation of the standard error estimates for each method to assess how stable these standard error estimates are.
These are the SEs of the $\widehat{SE}$s.
We can do this nested or overall, to look at both finite-sample and superpopulation performances.

We first calculate the ratio $stdev( \widehat{SE} )/ SE$, the standard deviation of the estimated standard errors to the true standard error.
We plot these ratios across simulation scenarios for each estimator below.
(For each estimator we only plot for the appropriate population context.)

We see that some methods (RIRC, FIRC, FE-CR, and the two superpopulation methods) are much more unstable with their standard error estimation, relative to the true size of their standard errors, than the other methods.
The site targeting estimators also have greater uncertaintly relative to their precisions than the person-targeting.
We leave determining whether this instability is compensated for correctly by degrees of freedom adjustments when generating confidence intervals or doing hypothesis testing for future work, but certaintly it points to lower power, if not invalidity.

The classic fixed effect methods (including the effectively similar method of RICC) have little to no variability in the precision of their nominal uncertainty estimation.
This is likely due to their standard errors being primarily dictated by the design matrix which is fixed across randomizations up to permutations, nested by site, of the rows (i.e., the only moving part is the column of treatment assignment dummies).
The rest of their standard errors is due to the estimate of the pooled standard deviation, which will generally be quite stable as it is assumes cross-site homogeniety.
By contrast, the Huber-White robust estimator is more variable as it does not impose a strong homosedasticity assumption and thus cannot take full advantage of the structure of the classic FE approaches.
Now in our simulations we actually *have* homoskedasticity, so this gain is appropriate.
We do not explore how wrong the SEs could be in the presence of residual heteroskedasticity.


```{r SD_SE, echo=FALSE}
srun2 = dplyr::select( sruns, method, weight, population, 
                       ID, J, n.bar, dependence, proptx.dependence, tau, 
                       sd.SE.hat.s, sd.SE.hat.f, SE.s, SE.f ) %>%
  mutate( sd.SE.hat.s = 100 * sd.SE.hat.s / SE.s,
          sd.SE.hat.f = 100 * sd.SE.hat.f / SE.f )
srun2 = mutate( srun2, sd.SE = ifelse( population=="finite", sd.SE.hat.f, sd.SE.hat.s ) )
ggplot( srun2, aes( x=method, y=sd.SE, fill=population ) ) +
#  facet_grid( ~ population ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip()+ 
  labs( y = "100*Ratio of Standard deviation of the standard errors to actual SEs", x="" )
```

To summarise this plot, we aggregate these across methods to create the following table:
```{r, echo=FALSE}
summ<- srun2 %>% group_by( method, weight, population ) %>% 
  summarise( mean.sd = mean(  sd.SE ),
          range.sd = get.interval( sd.SE, digits = 2 ) ) %>%
  arrange( population, weight )
knitr::kable(summ, digits=1 )
```

### Comparing DB-SP-Sites to FIRC

Because the FIRC true standard errors are generally smaller than DB-SP-Sites, comparing the uncertainty in the estimated standard errors directly is potentially confusing.
We instead compare the relative proportions, calculated above, between the two estimators.
We find that not only is the design based generally more unstable in truth, but that the estimates are also more unstable.
In particular, we see that the estimated SEs are, on average, 34% larger.


```{r SP_Site_v_FIRC_SE, echo=FALSE, results="hide", include=FALSE}
head( srun2 )
m2 = srun2 %>% dplyr::select( method, ID, J, n.bar, dependence, proptx.dependence, tau, sd.SE.hat.s ) %>%
  spread( method, sd.SE.hat.s )
head( m2 )
m2 = mutate( m2, ratio = `DB-SP-Sites` / FIRC )
ggplot( m2, aes( tau, ratio ) ) +
  facet_grid( dependence ~ proptx.dependence ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline( yintercept = 1 )
quantile( m2$ratio, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95 ) )
mean( m2$ratio )
```



## How often do the superpopulation estimators give lower SEs than finite population?

Superpopulation estimators have more variable uncertainty estimates, which allows them to quite frequently have smaller estimated SEs than a corresponding finite population estimator in scenarios with small amounts of cross-site impact variation.
For each scenario we counted what proportion of the time a superpopulation estimator's estimated SE was smaller than the design based DB-Finite-Persons' estimated SE.
And to see if these differences are substantial, we also plot the proportion of time the nominal superpopulation estimated SE was 10% or more smaller.
See figure below.
We see that, even with cross site variation amounts of around 0.10, we frequently see standard errors being smaller more than 25% of the time.
For very precisely estimated sites (more sites, or larger sites), this is less of a concern.

```{r SE_stability, echo=FALSE, results="hide"}

ggplot( filter( SE.comp.results, threshold %in% c("less", "way_less" ) ),
        aes( tau, I(100*percent), col=method, lty=threshold ) ) +
  facet_grid( J ~ n.bar, labeller = label_both ) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() +
  coord_cartesian( ylim=c(0,100) ) +
  geom_hline( yintercept=c(0,0.25), col="grey", size=0.3 )  +
  labs( x=expression(tau), y="Percent Chance") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(0,0.1, 0.2) ) +
  guides( lty=FALSE )

SE.comp.results %>% filter( tau == 0.1 ) %>% group_by( method, J, n.bar ) %>%
  summarise( per.less = mean( percent ) ) %>%
  spread( method, per.less )
```

The cluster-robust estimator, in particular, is quite unstable and can return very low standard errors.
The FIRC model, however, regularly returns lower standard errors, but very rarely undershoots the design based estimator by more than 10\%.
